title: REG U3·W3 — The Federal Estate & Generation-Skipping Tax (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the second half of the unified system

Last week's gift tax taxed lifetime transfers; the estate tax taxes the transfer at death, using the same unified exemption. When Jordan Reed dies, the executor files Form 706, totals everything Reed owned or controlled, subtracts deductions, and applies the unified credit. Because the exemption is so large, most estates owe nothing — but the computation, the inclusion surprises, and portability are squarely tested.

The gross estate

The gross estate is everything the decedent owned or controlled at death, valued at fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date six months later, if electing it lowers both the estate and the tax). It includes probate property, cash and securities (the MBG shares), real estate, and business interests — but the inclusion rules reach further than probate.

Inclusion rules that surprise

Several items pulled into the gross estate trip up candidates. Life insurance is included if the decedent owned the policy or held any incidents of ownership, or if proceeds are payable to the estate. Retained interests are caught: property the decedent transferred but kept a life estate (§2036) or the power to alter or revoke (§2038) is fully included. Gifts made within three years of death are generally not pulled back — except the gift tax paid on them (the gross-up rule) and transfers of life insurance. Jointly held property, general powers of appointment, and certain annuities are also included.

Deductions from the gross estate

From the gross estate the executor subtracts: funeral and administration expenses, the decedent's debts and unpaid taxes, casualty losses during administration, the unlimited marital deduction (property passing to a surviving U.S.-citizen spouse), the unlimited charitable deduction, and state death taxes. The marital deduction is the great deferral device — it pushes tax on the first spouse's estate to the death of the second.

From taxable estate to tax

The taxable estate is the gross estate minus deductions. To it the computation adds back post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts (so the brackets account for lifetime giving), produces a tentative tax at rates topping out near 40%, then subtracts gift taxes already paid and the unified credit. The credit shelters the basic exclusion amount — about $15 million per individual for 2026, made permanent and increased by Public Law 119-21 and indexed thereafter. Only estates above that exemption (net of lifetime gifts) actually owe tax.

Portability of the exemption

A spouse who dies without using the full exemption can pass the unused amount — the deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) — to the surviving spouse, who adds it to their own. Portability is not automatic: the executor must elect it on a timely filed Form 706, even for an estate too small to owe tax. With portability a married couple can shelter roughly twice the individual exemption without complex trust planning.

The generation-skipping transfer tax and the basis step-up

The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax is a separate, flat tax at the top rate layered on transfers that skip a generation — for example, a gift or bequest straight to a grandchild — to stop families from avoiding a layer of transfer tax. It has its own exemption (tracking the unified amount). Finally, the estate tax pairs with an income-tax benefit: property included in the gross estate gets a basis step-up to date-of-death fair market value, so heirs who later sell recognize gain only on post-death appreciation — the reason holding appreciated MBG stock until death can beat gifting it during life.

Putting it together on the family estate

Suppose Reed dies in 2026 with a $10 million gross estate, $1 million of debts and expenses, and $2 million passing to a spouse. The taxable estate is $10M − $1M − $2M (marital) = $7 million. Because that is well under the roughly $15 million exemption, the unified credit eliminates the tax entirely — and the executor may still file Form 706 to elect portability of the unused exemption to the surviving spouse, and the heirs take the assets with a stepped-up basis. The estate-and-gift system has taxed the transfer once, at a generous threshold, with the income tax forgiving the built-in gain.

Marital-deduction planning and estate liquidity

The unlimited marital deduction defers tax but does not erase it, so planning shapes how property passes to a spouse. A QTIP (qualified terminable interest property) trust lets the first spouse to die give the survivor a lifetime income interest while controlling who ultimately receives the property — and the estate elects to treat it as qualifying for the marital deduction, deferring tax to the survivor's death. A credit-shelter (bypass) trust instead uses the first spouse's exemption at the first death, keeping that amount and its future growth out of the survivor's estate; with portability now permanent many couples rely on the DSUE election, though a bypass trust still shelters post-death appreciation that portability does not.

Large estates also face a liquidity problem: estate tax is generally due nine months after death, yet much of a construction family's wealth may be illiquid business interests and real estate. §6166 lets an estate in which a closely held business exceeds 35% of the adjusted gross estate pay the tax in installments over up to fourteen years at a reduced interest rate — relief built precisely for a family business like MBG, so heirs need not fire-sale the company to pay the tax. The executor weighs this against the alternate valuation date and the deductions to settle the estate without dismantling it.

Filing, payment, and the alternate valuation election

The estate-tax return, Form 706, is generally due nine months after death (a six-month extension is available) and must be filed when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the exemption — or, for smaller estates, to elect portability. The executor may elect the alternate valuation date (six months after death) only if doing so decreases both the gross estate and the estate tax, which stops taxpayers from cherry-picking a higher basis without a tax cost; property sold or distributed during the six months is valued at that transaction date. These mechanics, with §6166 installments and the portability election, give the executor a toolkit to settle even an illiquid estate on time without dismantling the family business to raise cash.

CMA bridge

The gift tax (last week) and the estate tax (this week) draw on one unified exemption; together they decide how much of MBG's value Reed can move to the next generation tax-free. The date-of-death basis step-up ties back to FAR/REG property rules — the heir's basis in the inherited MBG stock is its FMV at death, not Reed's original cost.

Practice and recap

  1. Build the gross estate at date-of-death FMV (or alternate valuation); include life insurance with incidents of ownership, retained-interest transfers, and the gift tax on within-3-years gifts.
  2. Subtract debts/expenses and the unlimited marital and charitable deductions to reach the taxable estate.
  3. Add back adjusted taxable gifts, apply the ~40% rates, and shelter with the ~$15 million (2026, PL 119-21) unified credit.
  4. Elect portability of the DSUE on a timely Form 706; know the separate GST tax and the date-of-death basis step-up.

Recap: the estate tax totals everything the decedent owned or controlled (including life insurance with incidents of ownership and retained-interest transfers), subtracts the unlimited marital and charitable deductions, and shelters about $15 million per person for 2026 under Public Law 119-21; portability passes a spouse's unused exemption via a timely Form 706; the GST tax adds a flat top-rate layer on generation-skipping transfers; and inherited property takes a date-of-death basis step-up.

flashcards.back: Included if the decedent held any incidents of ownership or the proceeds are payable to the estate.

questions.q: Life insurance proceeds are included in the decedent's gross estate when the decedent:
choices: Held incidents of ownership in the policy
Bought the policy more than 3 years ago
questions.explain: Incidents of ownership (or proceeds payable to the estate) cause inclusion in the gross estate.

questions.q: The estate tax marital deduction for property passing to a surviving U.S.-citizen spouse is:
questions.explain: The marital deduction is unlimited, deferring tax until the surviving spouse's death.

questions.q: For 2026, the unified estate-and-gift exemption is approximately:
questions.explain: Public Law 119-21 set the basic exclusion at roughly $15 million per individual for 2026, indexed thereafter.

questions.q: Portability of a deceased spouse's unused exemption (DSUE):
choices: Requires a timely filed Form 706 election
Doubles the surviving spouse's income tax
questions.explain: Portability must be elected on a timely filed estate-tax return, even if no tax is due.

questions.q: Property included in the gross estate generally takes a basis equal to:
questions.explain: Inherited property is stepped to date-of-death FMV, so heirs are taxed only on later appreciation.

questions.q: The generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax applies to:
choices: Transfers that skip a generation (e.g., to a grandchild)
questions.explain: The GST tax is a separate flat top-rate tax on transfers skipping a generation.

questions.q: Gifts made within three years of death are generally:
choices: Not pulled back into the gross estate, except gift tax paid and life insurance
questions.explain: The three-year rule pulls back the gift tax paid (gross-up) and life-insurance transfers, but not most gifts themselves.
